claims.text: The Dolphin SDK is statically linked into every GameCube and Wii game, so once its functions are matched the remaining unmatched work in a new game is mostly game-specific code. The community already runs separate SDK decompilations for the 2001 and 2004 versions, which implies version-specific shared code is a recognised unit of reuse, though the sources give no measure of how much time it saves.

claims.text: Remaining byte differences fall into distinct categories that point to different causes: missing or extra instructions suggest branch or loop shape, wrong offsets suggest field layout or element size, and the same operations with different registers suggest declaration order or how long temporaries stay live. Different stack offsets or frame size point to local types, temporary structures or inlined helpers, so correct struct layouts do not rule out a mismatch. The guidance is to resolve instruction structure before operands, then register allocation, and not to rely on a percentage score alone.

claims.text: A function can still differ from the original because of things outside its own body: inline helpers, per-file pragmas, compiler version and flags, literal pools, string and constant layout, and section placement. Function-level similarity does not establish that the rebuilt file or final image matches, so full-binary comparison is the real completion test. Instruction-only checkers can also miss data differences.

claims.text: Without complete prototypes, the compiler applies default conversions and makes no attempt to check argument types or counts. A mismatch can cause arguments on the stack to be misread, corrupting not only the mismatched parameter but all subsequent ones. So partial type information does not just leave errors unreported; it lets wrong code compile and misbehave at runtime.

claims.text: Declaring a struct inside a function prototype makes the compiler scope it locally under strict ANSI mode, so the function can never be called without a type mismatch error. The fix is to declare the struct at global scope before the prototype. More type information therefore creates new mismatches when it is supplied in the wrong place or order, not only when it is wrong.

claims.text: Compilers detect errors, report them, and then try to recover so they can keep processing, and an undeclared identifier shows up as a missing symbol-table entry. A single missing shared definition therefore becomes an error in every file that uses it, and later errors may be recovery artifacts. GCC offers a limit on error count and an abort-on-first-error mode, which reflects that cascades are common enough to need controls.

claims.text: Padding is inserted automatically to satisfy alignment, so the total size of a structure is not the sum of its members. For the same members, reordering changes size from 24 bytes to 16 bytes, and turning padding off changes sizes from 4/8/24/16 to 3/7/13/13. A wrong width or padding assumption therefore compiles cleanly but yields a differently sized and shifted structure, which shows up as output or size differences rather than errors.

claims.text: Layout depends on the compiler's packing setting, which defaults to 8-byte packing in Microsoft's compiler and can be overridden per structure by directives. GCC also offers a Microsoft-compatible layout mode, and mixing its packing directive with its packed attribute may cause spurious warnings or unexpected behavior. Identical source can therefore produce different binaries depending on settings, so differences may come from build configuration rather than a reconstruction error.
